posts.text:
I have been asked about 24 hour trading a lot recently.  

For most stocks on most days it won't matter much because the overnight volume is likely to be low relative to regular trade hours (RTH)

For stocks with a catalyst that causes large volume outside of RTH,  it makes sense to include that price and volume action.

Notice how the price of $NVDA reacted to the Sunday night open of the stock vs the RTH.

The black VWAP includes the 24 hour session and the red is just RTH.  There was significant volume (esp premarket) but you can see how the RTH volume opening bar made the overnight nearly irrelevant.

About an hour into day, the 2 vwaps converged (red circle) and then traded pretty much identically.

We see this same action each day with $ES_F - most days the overnight VWAP is quickly overwhelmed by the 930am VWAP.

There are unusual times when it makes sense to be aware of both because the overnight range was large enough and came with enough volume to still hold significance

These are my evolving thoughts which are likely to shift as the market gives us more feedback on 24 hr trading.

On a side note, the TradingView colors of sessions remind me of ice cream

http://CNBC.com - 11/9/2026

- Nvidia's investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a purported Chinese spy has raised questions about whether he may be forced to step back from leading the chipmaker.

- Huang is practically synonymous with Nvidia, which he co-founded in 1993 and turned into one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., during the Nvidia GTC conference in San Jose, California, US, on Wednesday, March 18, 2026.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admission of an affair with a purported Chinese spy has raised questions about his future at the company, and what happens if the 63-year-old co-founder, who built the chipmaker into one of the most valuable businesses on the planet, is forced out.

Shares of Nvidia sank more than 5% on Monday, even as the broader market rallied sharply, after Huang acknowledged the affair in a message to staff on Sunday, and said that the board was launching an investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence agency. The board said it has "confidence in Jensen," and that it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

The New York Times first reported that the Chinese businesswoman was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the intelligence circulated in a memo among the Trump administration in the spring. China has called the allegation a smear.

While Nvidia says Huang will continue to lead the company during the probe, pressure is rapidly mounting on the chipmaker, whose technology has powered the first four years of the generative artificial intelligence boom. Leaders from both parties are calling for briefings, and Democrats poised to take control of both houses of Congress are calling for investigations and new legislation "to stop advanced AI chips from fueling China's military," Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts wrote in a post on X on Monday.

Huang has outsized influence over Nvidia, and is the sole face of the company with no clear second-in-command. He's also among the loudest champions of AI in the country, is critical to the financing of the broader infrastructure buildout and has a close relationship with President Donald Trump, giving Nvidia a front-row seat when it comes to discussions on AI policy, safety and regulation.

"The issue at Nvidia is that there is no clear successor to Jensen, and we had expected him to stay in this role for at least 10 more years," analysts at Melius Research said in a Monday research note.

Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Monday that, "Jensen is Nvidia. Nvidia is Jensen." He added that Huang "runs the thing pretty much top down," and "sort of pulls all the strings."

Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nvidia has long maintained a flat, non-hierarchical organizational structure. Huang has deep involvement in the company's day-to-day operations, with around 60 direct reports, and frequently serves as its spokesperson in front of world leaders and at industry conferences. In addition to being co-founder and CEO, Huang is also Nvidia's president.

A 28-year-old UMass graduate student got a homework assignment to reproduce a famous economics paper, couldn't make the numbers match, and found a spreadsheet mistake in a study that politicians had used to argue for budget cuts.

His name is Thomas Herndon.

In 2010, two Harvard economists, Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff, published a short paper called Growth in a Time of Debt. Its headline finding: once a country's public debt goes above 90% of its economy, growth falls off a cliff. In their numbers, average growth for that group was minus 0.1%.

It came out right after the 2008 financial crisis, and it spread fast. In the US, the Paul Ryan budget cited it as its only evidence on what high debt does to growth.

In Europe, an EU commissioner pointed to the research in a speech. In Britain, George Osborne cited the authors by name.

Herndon was a PhD student at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, taking a class called Econ 753: Applied Econometrics. The big assignment was to pick a well-known paper and replicate it.

He picked this one. He couldn't get the same results.

He asked the authors for their spreadsheet, and they sent it. When he spotted the problem, he called his girlfriend over to make sure he wasn't seeing things.

He wasn't.

Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success," Nvidia says.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
This can only be settled in the streets. Nick gets to fight with a calculator though because Corey’s endurance is obviously unfair.

In all seriousness, I think this debate is built on a false premise. There’s no such thing as “passive” investing. Everyone deviates from the global market cap portfolio. The S&P 500 is a committee-picked large cap US stock fund. Choosing it is an active decision. Your stock/bond mix is an active decision. Rebalancing is an active decision. Blah blah blah. You prob know my rant by now.

So the real question isn’t active vs. passive. It’s low fee, low turnover and rules-based vs. high fee, high turnover and discretionary. And then whether any of it actually fits the investor’s planning needs.

There are silly index funds and very good ones. SPY is a great one IMO. It’s cheap, diversified and lets winners run while losers shrink. It doesn’t so much distort prices as accept the prices set by more active investors at the margin. And there are lots of great active deviations from it too. Indexing isn’t the end all be all, especially now that you can run a smart active strategy in an ETF for close to index fund fees.

Aggregate bond index funds are a great example of a flawed methodology, yet people revere them for no real reason other than cheap diversification. They’re weighted by how much debt issuers sell, so the biggest borrowers get the biggest weights. Their duration drifts based on what the Treasury and corporations decide to issue, not on anything the investor needs. And because bonds trade far less than stocks, index rules matter more. Look at the forced selling when bonds get downgraded out of investment grade indexes. They borrow market cap logic from stocks, where it makes sense, and apply it to debt, where it doesn’t. That can distort prices and serves the end investor poorly.

Funny thing is the critics usually aim at the wrong target. Broad equity index funds are generally great. It’s the bond indexes that make less sense. So Nick is right that equity indexing is a huge win for investors, and Corey is right that index methodology can distort prices. They’re just talking past each other in a debate that’s a lot more nuanced than either side admits.

The math is fine. The accounting is wrong.

When a fund pays out 11%, its price drops by that amount. That's not income. It's a withdrawal with less control over taxes and timing than selling shares yourself.

What matters is total return. If the fund earns 6% and pays 11%, you're eating 5% of your principal every year. The "paycheck" shrinks each year and inflation and taxes make it worse. Those yields usually come from covered calls or return of capital, which cap your upside and leave you with the downside. 

Take the popular "distribution Yield" funds for example. QQQI sells call options on the Nasdaq 100. That premium is the "income," but it means handing someone else your gains above a certain level. You keep the downside and give up part of the upside thinking you got safer "income" when you actually locked in a lower total return. 

And the upside is where stock returns come from, usually in a few sharp rallies after selloffs. In April 2026 alone, QQQ returned about 15.7% to QQQI's 10.3%. Add a 0.68% fee versus 0.18% for QQQ and it falls further behind. It wins in flat markets, but the longer you hold the longer you give up the compound upside trend. 

Here's the actual "paycheck" result using the OP example. Both accounts paid out the exact same paychecks on the exact same days. The one that "sold shares" just has more left because it didn't pay the high fees or cap its upside with covered call "income".

The Biggest Risk Is Human

After $6.3 billion in crypto was stolen from Binance, the conversation quickly and understandably turned to how investors hold scarce assets such as gold and, especially, crypto. Where does the fund store its physical gold? How is its bitcoin secured?

Fair questions. But to understand what the Binance theft tells us about custody, it helps to look at how the attackers got in.

According to Binance’s preliminary investigation, one of its engineers applied for what looked like a real job. The company was fictitious. The coding assignment contained malware. That was one step in a months-long attack that ultimately drained internet-connected wallets at the exchange.

That fake hiring process is a textbook example of social engineering. The attackers used a believable job opportunity, hence human gullibility, to get an engineer to run malicious code.

Today, Nvidia announced an independent investigation into whether foreign intelligence targeted its CEO, Jensen Huang.

Huang acknowledged an affair. Several media outlets reported that U.S. officials believed the woman involved was a Chinese intelligence asset. China denies the allegation. Nvidia’s board said it had no reason at that point to believe company secrets had been compromised.

The Nvidia investigation is still open, but the allegations put the Binance story in a broader context. A job interview can get someone to run a piece of code. A relationship can give someone access to a person with sensitive information. What happens from there depends on what that person can access, share, or authorize.

In traditional finance, we see examples all the time. In 2024, 26 financial firms agreed to pay nearly $393 million in SEC penalties for failing to preserve electronic communications. That was a serious control failure. How many investors read those headlines and asked whether their stocks and bonds were properly held in custody?

The same distinction matters when we talk about bitcoin in cold storage or physical gold in a Swiss vault. Where and how the assets are held shapes what an attacker can reach. Who can authorize a transfer or release, and how that instruction is verified, shapes what they can move.

Both deserve continuous scrutiny. Review who has access. Test how transfer instructions are verified. Check what happens when someone tries to bypass a control. That work is especially important in bitcoin custody, where the technology and the ways attackers exploit it keep changing.

Yet, even the best technology depends on the judgment of the people who use it. A convincing recruiter or a familiar voice can get us to make a mistake the technology was never designed to catch.
